newsitem.title: USA: Most dikes hold up in U.S. northern plains flood area.
newsitem.headline: Most dikes hold up in U.S. northern plains flood area.

text.p: The overflowing Red River crested in Fargo more than 20 feet above flood stage, and officials said Saturday the dikes and sandbags holding back the floodwaters were largely intact.
But as temperatures warmed, melting snow raised concern about another possible crest as water levels remained at historically high levels.

"The river is cresting," said Dennis Walaker, director of operations at the Fargo engineering department. "We're still concerned a little bit about runoff. There's still a tremendous amount of water against the sandbags."
The Red River, which forms the border of North Dakota and Minnesota, crested in Fargo at about 37.6 feet (11.5 meters), officials said. Flood stage is at 17 feet (5.2 meters).
"All clay dikes are in good condition," Walaker said. "We continue to have isolated problems with sandbag dikes and private homes."
He said the city had three truckloads full of sandbags ready to be sent out to plug leaks.
Officials said the river level was slowly beginning to drop, particularly in the southern part of Fargo, but the threat of a second crest and more flooding remained.

"We still have a lot of snow out there and as the temperatures continue to rise now through next week, that's going to melt and we're going to have a lot of overland water," said Capt. Patrick Richards of North Dakota's Emergency Management division.
"We're not out of the woods here by any means," he said. "We're going to have several days of very, very high water out there and it's going to remain high."
Donald Schwert, a geologist at North Dakota State University, said flood stage conditions in Fargo would likely remain for several days.
"There's still a lot of water to move through Fargo," he said. "Theres a lot of water south of Fargo in the Red River valley in the tributaries that still has to pass through."

Walaker said the river level had dropped about 4 inches 6 miles south of Fargo, but it would take a drop of 7 to 8 feet (2.1 to 2.4 meters) before people could begin to move back to their homes to assess damage.
He added that if daytime temperatures hold to the low- to mid-40s (5-10 Celsius), overnight freezing should help keep the floodwaters under control.
"The best scenario is for the river to drop a little bit to lessen some of the problems," he said.
